Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI
abstract: Last year, we introduced GEM , the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions. The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for. GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers. GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas: 1. Bending the Scaling Curve, Enabling 2.5x Model Complexity Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions. Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun , co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results. 2. Efficient Intelligence Transfer From GEM to User-Facing Models Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI. Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM , a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation ( Solaris ) to harvest the gains from the upstream model. 3. Accelerating the Central Compute Engine With Large-Scale Cross-Surface, Cross-Domain Learning at Meta Ads Scale Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously. title: OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks
abstract: At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube). Launching the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) initiative within OCP. We’re inviting engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in meeting the challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI infrastructure. At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011. Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative. This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone . Here’s some of what’s new: The 102.4T scale-out switch : Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack) and 102.4T switch blades (IceCube), designed to support high power density, deliver higher thermal efficiency, and enable gigawatt-scale AI clusters. The scale-out Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) : Meta’s multiplane fabric, enabling larger, highly efficient GPU clusters with lower latency — with learnings shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across for multi-site clusters : Meta’s petabit-scale backend aggregation (BAG) super-spine and how large-scale training jobs deal with failures at this scale — with an overview of how we’ve built SRv6 regional backbones using FBOSS and SAI to handle even longer distances Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking: Meta’s MTIA 300 system uses Tahan, an Ethernet-based 51.2T scale-up switch, delivering 6.4 Tbps per accelerator — with a preview of next-gen 72-accelerator-per-rack design on 102.4T silicon and moving toward an ESUN-based implementation with future chips. MetaRoCE : Meta’s RDMA transport protocol for AI networks — now with open-source implementations. title: Shipping Media Over QUIC at Meta Scale for Instagram Live Ingest
abstract: Meta has begun deploying Media over QUIC (MoQ), an emerging open protocol for real-time video streaming at scale. MoQ will help simplify our protocol stack for live streaming video and enhance overall user experience for live video. We’re sharing how we shipped MoQ on Instagram Live ingest, and what the future looks like from here. This work was also presented at DEMOQED 2026 . Instagram Live now uses the open standard transport protocol Media over QUIC (MoQ) for live video ingest on iOS and Android. As a transport designed for both ingest and playback, MoQ gives us the foundation to build toward an architecture that is lower-latency, more resilient on unreliable networks, and more responsive for creators and viewers. It also gives teams across Meta a common foundation for bringing those improvements to future live and interactive experiences without rebuilding them on separate protocol stacks. MoQ: A Media Protocol for Every Moment in Time The internet has accumulated a rich set of media protocols, each shaped by the problem in front of it. RTMP for ingestion. HLS and DASH for playback. WebRTC for real-time calls. RUSH for the cases that did not fit neatly into any of those. Each was a strong answer for its moment, and together they’ve carried the industry a long way. At Meta, someone who starts a live stream and then makes a voice call on the same app touches three different protocol stacks, each with its own serving infrastructure, monitoring, and operational expertise. That separation made sense when these experiences were distinct. But as live video, real-time AI, and generative AI creation tools increasingly share the same product surface, the lines between these use cases are starting to blur. A common protocol across ingest, delivery, and playback can reduce the number of custom transports and operating models that engineering teams need to maintain and improve over time. How MoQ Works MoQ is an emerging IETF standard that enables low-latency, scalable media delivery (live streaming, real-time communication) over the QUIC transport layer. It’s being developed collaboratively at the IETF, with active participation from Meta, Google, Akamai, Cisco, Cloudflare, and academia. For nearly a decade, Meta’s live streaming video has run on Reliable Ultra-low-latency Streaming over HTTP (RUSH), an in-house QUIC-based protocol built to move past RTMP. RUSH proved that QUIC could carry live media at scale and was a predecessor to MoQ. The lessons learned from running RUSH in production are part of what shaped our bet on MoQ. The core abstraction in MoQ is a Track , an addressable stream of media objects that publishers push and subscribers receive through a network of relays. Relays cache and forward objects without parsing the media payload – they only need to understand the MoQ framing and delivery metadata. A few properties matter for using MoQ as a single transport across the full latency spectrum: Built on QUIC: QUIC lets independent streams make progress without TCP-style cross-stream head-of-line blocking. It also supports faster connection setup and connection migration. Meta’s earlier QUIC rollout achieved lower request errors, tail latency, and video stalls than HTTP/2. MoQ applies the same transport foundation to live and real-time media. MoQ would also automatically benefit from any feature added to QUIC (e.g., FEC). Native Fan-out and caching: MoQ relays are built-in caching and request/stream coalescing endpoints, so media streams scale through CDN relays out of the box. Request coalescing, caching, and fan-out are not new (live streaming already does them), but MoQ makes them part of the protocol design rather than a bolt-on, and it is designed to scale via relays more efficiently than traditional HTTP streaming. title: Turning Opportunistic AI Inference Capacity Into Better Ads Recommendations
abstract: At Meta, we’ve built a system that enhances ads recommendations by leveraging idle inference capacity in our fleet. Two elasticity levers in the system allow ads recommendation work to expand across opportunistic capacity, without compromising baseline performance. This post describes how we designed and now operate the system at Meta’s scale and how it drives significant advertiser value and capacity efficiency. Inference fleets face a capacity paradox: They can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta, we built a system that aggregates these pockets into a shared opportunistic capacity pool and turns them into better ads recommendations. By putting otherwise idle capacity to work, the system helps people see more relevant ads and improves advertiser outcomes without requiring additional capacity orders. Using this opportunistic capacity safely is difficult. It’s distributed across team-owned capacity allocations, regions, and accelerator types, and may be reclaimed with little notice. The ads inference system must therefore adapt workload as capacity supply changes without overloading the dedicated capacity that serves baseline workload. We address this challenge with two complementary elasticity levers. Rank More Ads (RMA) adjusts the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages. Serve Better Models (SBM) adjusts the share of requests routed to a more powerful model. Physical and logical isolation protects the capacity reserved for baseline serving. Separate feedback loops control RMA candidate volume and SBM model coverage, while value-aware load shedding at both servers and clients allows the system to degrade gracefully when capacity is suddenly reclaimed. Together, these mechanisms allow optional work to expand and contract with opportunistic capacity while protecting latency and reliability. The Inference Capacity Paradox: Globally Constrained, but Locally Idle Inference fleets must maintain enough capacity to meet demand under strict latency and reliability targets. However, demand and capacity rarely align perfectly across time, regions, resource combinations, and accelerator types. Capacity can therefore remain idle in parts of a fleet even when the fleet is constrained overall. Common causes include: Peak-provisioning and demand-variation mismatch: Inference fleets must be provisioned for peak demand, while traffic varies by time of day and season. Capacity needed during peak periods can therefore remain temporarily idle when demand is lower. Model-development and capacity-delivery timing mismatch: Inference capacity arrives on supply-chain timelines, whereas models are developed and launched on separate schedules. This creates a gap between when capacity becomes available and when models are ready to consume it. Regional resource-ratio mismatch: Inference workloads require accelerators as well as supporting resources such as CPUs. When these resources are not available in the required proportions, one resource can remain idle while another limits serving capacity. Accelerator-type mismatch: Inference fleets can span multiple accelerator vendors, generations, and architectures. Workloads are not always portable across these accelerator types, which can strand capacity on hardware that cannot immediately serve the available demand. These mismatches create an industry-wide inference capacity paradox: A fleet can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta’s scale, these temporary pockets can collectively represent substantial capacity and create better ads recommendations when used safely. title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
abstract: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Figure 1: AI tutors need feedback from students to improve. Student simulators can approximate part of that feedback during research-stage training and evaluation. They provide an early-stage research signal, not a replacement for testing with real learners. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. title: Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch?
abstract: AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. GKA uniquely offers variable-length inference computation without retraining and gives the user direct control over its position on the speed-accuracy frontier. A good lossy summary of everything beats a perfect recording of the most recent past. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWA), even when SWA gets twice the memory budget. Same quality, twice the throughput. A 32-billion-parameter GKA-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context and reaching correct answers in as little as two-thirds of the wall-clock time. To foster further research on hybrid architectures, we have released a zoo of primed hybrid models at the eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scales for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with training code, optimized kernels, and a vLLM-serving plugin under the Apache 2.0 License. The attention mechanism A Transformer’s attention mechanism — which determines how relevant previously seen tokens are to the token currently being processed — relies on three different vectors, which take their names from database design: the query, the key, and the value. For each token, the query captures what that token is “looking for,” the key captures what it “offers,” and the value carries the actual information it will pass along. Relevance is computed by comparing the current token’s query against every other token’s key; the closer the match, the more that token’s value contributes to the output of attention. Each of these vectors is produced by multiplying the token by a learned weight projection matrix. title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent . Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors. In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can: Deploy a multi-agent IDP system, often in under 20 minutes. Process new document types without manual template configuration. Let agents train themselves on each new document format and reuse what they learn, so later documents of that type go straight to extraction without retraining. Challenges with rule-based document processing Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges: Template rigidity: Each new document format requires manual configuration, and even minor layout changes can cause extraction failures. No learning: The same extraction errors repeat across similar documents because the system doesn’t retain knowledge from previous corrections. Scaling burden: Each new vendor or document variant multiplies the maintenance effort, and organizations processing documents from hundreds of sources face ongoing operational costs. An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration. Automation workflow (known document types): When a match is found, the Extractor agent uses existing instructions. If validation fails, the Troubleshooter agent fixes the extracted data directly without modifying instructions. title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets. Solution overview The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content. The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control. Key concepts This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution. Agent orchestration with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic. The supervisor agent exposes two tools: generate_pptx: Creates PowerPoint presentations by invoking the PPTX Generator Lambda function, which retrieves content from the knowledge base, generates slide outlines, creates AI images, and assembles the final document. generate_summary: Extracts and synthesizes information from the knowledge base using RAG to deliver accurate, grounded responses. The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses. title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. About Tamnoon Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. Cloud security remediation challenges A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Alert volume overwhelms headcount: CNAPPs and scanners generate thousands of findings. Teams can’t triage them all, so critical exposures sit unresolved while risk compounds for months. Investigation is manual and repetitive: Each finding requires context gathering on who owns the resource, what depends on it, whether the fix is safe. This eats hours of senior engineer time, repeated across every item in the backlog. Fear of production impact blocks automation: Teams hesitate to automate remediation because they can’t risk taking down production. Without confidence that a fix is safe, nothing moves. Reactive prioritization: Without a way to cluster related findings or score remediation confidence, teams work through alerts linearly rather than addressing root causes that resolve many issues at once. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Solution overview Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. title: Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Choosing the right model for a specific application requires a practical way to test it with representative inputs. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides access to a broad catalog of already pretrained models. In this post, we show how to deploy an available model from SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete. For supported models and available capacity, this workflow provides a repeatable evaluation path, although deployment time varies by model, instance type, quota, and AWS Region. In 2026, SageMaker JumpStart introduced two improvements that simplify model discovery and deployment. In the Model Hub section of the Amazon SageMaker AI console, you can browse the SageMaker JumpStart catalog, view sample notebooks, and open them directly in SageMaker Studio. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options provide named configurations optimized for priorities such as low cost, low latency, or general-purpose workloads across a range of generative AI models, including Neuron-optimized configurations. Additionally, you can now go from Hugging Face model discovery to SageMaker AI deployment in a single click using the new deep link integration. title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
abstract: AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention. Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory , it’s now available on AWS Marketplace . This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction. Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch. When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption. Challenges When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention. Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent. abstract: Managing AI model access across dozens or hundreds of AWS accounts creates operational friction when each workload account must subscribe and accept AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers (MPPOs) individually. Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements simplifies multi-account access to third-party AI models so you can subscribe once from a central account and distribute access across your organization. In this post, we show you two ways to activate AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offer (MPPO) entitlements in AWS License Manager. Use the lightweight script when you want a one-time, no-infrastructure fix for received licenses you already trust. Use the CDK automation when you want ongoing event-driven processing that verifies sellers, creates and activates distributed grants. Why automate grant activation With AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers, you can negotiate custom rates for third-party models on Amazon Bedrock. After an eligible private offer is accepted, AWS Marketplace creates a license in AWS License Manager. In AWS Organizations with all features enabled, organization-level grants are auto-accepted but remain Disabled until you activate them. Teams often manage this by checking the AWS License Manager console and activating grants manually. Manual checks work, but they add effort and are easy to miss. Until someone activates the grant, negotiated pricing does not apply. The same effort appears as teams adopt new models or renew terms. It only creates and activates organization-wide grants when you re-run it with --apply --confirm-account-id . It has no seller allow-list, so use it only when you trust every received license in the management account. Path 2 – The event-driven path uses AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy ongoing automation in your AWS management account. Choose one of the following implementation paths. title: Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain-specific query languages. Orca Security ’s tool covers over 900 cloud models (the resource types Sonar tracks, such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance or an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket). Querying that data required precise model names, nested relationship navigation, and selection from 18 operators (comparison functions like equals or contains used to filter results). To solve this, Orca Security partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a natural language query agent on Amazon Bedrock . Orca provides context-aware security for cloud, code, and AI, and Sonar is its domain-specific query system where users search, filter, and explore across the entire data graph. In this post, we share the architecture and results of Discovery AI, which converts a natural language question into a Sonar query. As a result, Orca reduced query costs by 90 percent, input tokens by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. Bridging natural language and structured queries Orca Security’s Sonar query system supports 900+ cloud infrastructure and application models with complex relationships between them. To query this data, users construct JSON objects that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent-child hierarchies across cloud providers. Doing this well requires deep familiarity with the Sonar schema. To build this capability, the Orca team set out to build a natural language interface that can generate valid Sonar queries from plain text. Their initial proof of concept loaded the full Sonar schema into a single prompt on the largest available model. This included over 900 model definitions, every relationship type, and a generous set of example queries. The output quality was strong (design partners and internal users responded positively) but three significant drawbacks emerged at production scale. Token consumption was inefficient, at roughly 2 million input tokens per workload, which drove up cost. Latency was high, with end-to-end response times of around 60 seconds per workload. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries was limited because nested relationships and multi-condition queries often required additional refinement. The Orca team validated that the concept worked. The next challenge was making it cost-effective, fast, and accurate enough for production. To address this, the Orca team designed and deployed a solution that handles thousands of queries per day at 15-second response times using Amazon Bedrock. Solution overview Orca designed Discovery AI as a hybrid solution on Amazon Bedrock that combines Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with schema-aware query construction. The system converts natural language questions into valid Discovery filters through a multi-stage pipeline, with each stage matched to the most appropriate Amazon Bedrock model. Orca chose Amazon Bedrock because it provides multi-model access through a single API, letting the team allocate different foundation models to each pipeline stage without managing separate integrations. Amazon Bedrock also inherits AWS governance controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints, and AWS CloudTrail, meeting Orca’s security requirements. The model-agnostic architecture meant the team could swap in newer model versions as they became available without rearchitecting the pipeline. abstract: This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Banh, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global. Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand , an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 is trained to work longer on more difficult tasks and knows when to check its own work. That matters most for agents, which carry a task through many steps and must verify what they find along the way. An agent that works this way has to do more than look things up. It has to form a candidate answer, check it against what it has learned, and refine it until it fits. Grok 4.7 exposes a reasoning effort setting that controls how much deliberation happens before each response, and for agent workloads a practical question is which level to run. In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three tasks that require search rather than lookup. The tasks are diagnosing a two-service outage from its alerts, scheduling maintenance under interacting constraints, and choosing an optimal set of migrations under a budget. Each task has exactly one correct answer, verified by brute force. We ran all three at every reasoning effort level, six times each, for 72 agent runs. The agent answered 67 of the 72 runs correctly. title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains. Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations. In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example. Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle. This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid. This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation: A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N] Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension. During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout: Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096). Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192). Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization. In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. abstract: Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure. This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 . In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . You then extend the same runtime with SemIf , formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Solution overview Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model , maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions , and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments. The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter. Reply with the best support queue." } ], "max_tokens": 64, "stream": false } The response uses the OpenAI-compatible choices array. Read generated text from choices[0].message.content . SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options: { "decision": { "id": "support-route", "state": "The customer cannot receive a password reset email.", "question": "Which queue should handle this request?", "options": [ {"id": "account_access", "description": "Account access support."}, {"id": "billing", "description": "Billing support."} ] } } The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. abstract: This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers . It uses separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This kind of multi-node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads. In a previous post , we introduced the Ray Serve DLC and used it to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node. You had a working inference endpoint, and the container keeps the GPU stack compatible, including CUDA libraries, so you did not need to write boilerplate code. Ray is a distributed compute framework, so Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes. Customers use multi-node Ray Serve for several reasons. Some want to run foundation or open-weight models that are too large for a single GPU. Others need more throughput than one replica can deliver. Still others want to separate the two phases of inference to improve performance. In each case, customers must build the dependency chain themselves: choosing compatible libraries for the GPU stack and debugging issues when a component drifts out of alignment. This is undifferentiated work that takes time and effort away from delivering models. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) have long solved this kind of problem for training and inferencing workloads. DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. With the launch of the Ray LLM DLC for multi-node deployments, that same approach now extends to multi-node inference. You get a container purpose-built for serving models behind an HTTP endpoint, maintained and tested by AWS, with the full inference stack already assembled. This post walks through implementing multi-node disaggregated inference using multi-node Ray LLM DLC: deploying a single large language model across two GPU-powered nodes on Amazon EKS cooperating behind a single endpoint. While one of the GPU nodes handles the prefill phase, the other GPU node handles the decode phase. Separating the phases prevents compute-heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress. This approach is well suited for workloads such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), document summarization, and agentic applications. We use the multi-node Ray LLM DLC, which ships Ray Serve LLM , NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) , and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with no application code. The complete code is available in the accompanying repository . Why prefill/decode (PD) disaggregation LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds the key-value (KV) cache. Decode then generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending that cache. Prefill is compute bound, and Decode is bound by memory bandwidth. When both phases share one GPU, they contend for the same resources, and the bursty, compute-heavy prefill work interferes with the steady, latency-sensitive decode work. Separating the prefill phase from the decode phase means you can select the hardware and serving properties for each phase, improving overall performance at scale. PD disaggregation places the two phases on separate nodes, so each phase runs without interfering with the other and can be scaled independently. The trade-off is that the KV cache built during prefill must be handed to the decode node, and that transfer should be fast enough not to erase the benefit. That is exactly why the interconnect between the nodes matters. abstract: Authors: Divya Gadde , Ko-Jen Hsiao , Dhaval Patel and Moumita Bhattacharya The motivation for building the Netflix Foundation Model for personalization was laid out in this previous blog post. The Netflix homepage is powered by several specialized models and it requires significant time and resources to maintain and continue innovating on these individual models. Therefore, we decided to centralize member preference learning and have one powerful model learned from comprehensive user interaction histories and content data at a large scale and have this model distribute its learnings to other models. The previous two blog posts( 1 , 2 ) focus on the development of the Foundation Model and here we talk about how we integrate the Foundation Model into various applications. We found that there is extensive literature focused on the training and inference of large-scale transformer-based models. However, there remains a significant gap in practical guidance and research on how to effectively and efficiently integrate large models into existing production systems. At Netflix, we experimented with 3 distinct integration approaches — embeddings, subgraph and fine-tuning. The motivation for trying different approaches stems from varying application needs. Specifically, different teams have different latency requirements, tech stack constraints and different appetites for leveraging the full power of a large foundation model. In this blog, we go over the 3 approaches we experimented with and which are now used in production for different use cases. Each integration approach has its own set of motivations, tradeoffs, complexities and learnings. The following sections go into the details of each of these integration approaches. Embeddings from Foundation model Transformer style foundation models naturally lend themselves to generating comprehensive user profile and item representations. Our approach for generating embeddings includes getting the hidden state of the last user event as the profile embedding and weights from the item tower as item embeddings. Netflix has an elaborate set up for refreshing the embeddings every day. First, the Foundation Model is pre-trained from scratch every month. Then, the monthly pre-trained model is fine-tuned everyday based on the latest data. The daily fine-tuning also expands the entity id space to include the newly launching titles. After the daily fine-tuned model is ready, we run batch inference to refresh the profile and item embeddings and publish them to the Embedding Store. An important part of this setup is the embedding stabilization technique ( paper ). When the pretraining job retrains the model from scratch, the embedding spaces between different runs are completely different due to the random initialization in the model. In addition, the embeddings start to drift when the daily job fine-tunes on the latest data, despite the daily fine-tuning job warm-starting from the previous day’s model. Therefore, it is important to map the embeddings generated everyday into the same embedding space, so that downstream models can consume pre-computed embeddings as features. This embedding approach relies heavily on the Embedding Store, which is a feature store specializing in embeddings built by the platform team at Netflix. The embedding store makes producing and consuming embeddings easy by taking care of versioning and timestamping the embeddings. The Embedding Store also provides various interfaces to access the embeddings offline and online. title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
abstract: by Olek Gorajek , Samuel Redai , Yian Shang Intro Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets. Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values. Initial Problem Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required: extensive business knowledge familiarity with experimentation conventions and complex engineering practices This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform. Enter DataJunction To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case. DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers ( Beto Dealmeida ), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet , have been building out the remaining features of the platform. title: Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations
abstract: By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan Kallus Introduction Personalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog. But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time? In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings. The Measurement Challenge A natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand. The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences. One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy. Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence. A Model of Member Choice To measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see. A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. abstract: By Oleksii Tkachuk , Rajiv Shringi , Chris Lohfink , Abe Ratnofsky , Kartik Sathyanarayanan Introduction In an earlier post , we introduced the TimeSeries Abstraction, our high-throughput, low-latency platform designed to store and query temporal event data at scale. It has since become the operational backbone for Netflix’s largest datasets, which now span multiple petabytes. However, managing such large datasets in hot storage, tuned for low-millisecond latency access , is not cheap. At Netflix, cost-efficiency is a continuous discipline rather than a temporary initiative. This post shares two solutions that significantly reduce storage costs by continuously moving older, less frequently accessed data into cheaper object storage: Solution 1 : Uses Apache Kafka and Flink to stream data directly to S3 Solution 2 : Leverages Cassandra backups in S3 and pluggable Memtables to read data directly from S3 We’ll start with the Kafka/Flink-based design, then describe how we evolved to a native Cassandra-based cold tier. Challenges As Netflix’s TimeSeries datasets have expanded, we’ve encountered several compounding challenges: Growing retention demands : Users often push for increasing data retention to serve a broader range of use cases, which in turn increases the storage costs. Escalating costs : Maintaining massive, dense clusters for infrequently accessed historical data is prohibitively expensive. Sparse historical access: Most queries target recent events, but older data must remain readily available for occasional audits and investigations. Operational strain : High storage density on hot nodes complicates scaling, deployment, and cluster stability. Latency requirements : Even historical data sometimes requires sub-second query performance for internal tooling and analysis. This creates a clear opportunity: keep the most recent data on fast storage and migrate older, rarely read data to cheaper storage while preserving a consistent API . Done well, this can meet user and operational needs while greatly reducing our infrastructure spend. Time Slices and Immutable Windows This enables several key optimizations, most notably allowing a table to become immutable once it crosses the write boundary, which lets us safely apply further optimizations. For more details, refer to our previous post . This slice information is critical and is maintained in a dedicated metadata table: Time Slice Metadata Storage Creating new Time Slices and maintaining their metadata is a primary responsibility of the TimeSeries control plane. abstract: By Yogesh Nagarur Introduction In Part 1 of this series , we shared how Netflix built the Ads Event pipeline and approached it as a system design problem: replacing fragmented pipelines with a centralized collection, enrichment, and a standard data contract. The result was Ads Event Publisher, the system that collects ad telemetry from client devices, enriches it with the context of the ad that was actually served, and publishes a single, unified stream of ad events to every downstream consumer: frequency capping, metrics, billing, measurement partners, and reporting. Any member viewing or account details that move through this pipeline end-to-end are encrypted and handled in accordance with Netflix’s strict privacy and security practices to safeguard member PII. If ad serving is the “brain” and ad events are the “heartbeats” that feed it, then enrichment is what gives each heartbeat its meaning, turning a bare “[Somebody] watched an ad to completion” signal into “ this campaign, this creative, at this price, for this break.” Part 1 described that enrichment step as a single box in the architecture. This post is about what was inside that box, and why we rebuilt it. Part 1 ended with a look at what was on the horizon: ads on live streams, de-duplication, and richer data signals. A single project delivered all three by rebuilding the Ads Event Publisher around stateful stream processing. We replaced a database lookup with a real-time streaming join in Apache Flink, which let the system scale for Live, took a dependency off the critical path, and replaced the engine of a high-traffic pipeline without downtime. Let’s dive in. A quick recap: enrichment and the Metadata Registry When an ad is served, the ad server knows everything about it: the campaign, the creative, the price of the impression, the targeting context, and the tracking URLs that measurement partners expect us to fire. The client device, by contrast, knows almost nothing: just an opaque token and when to send each event. Enrichment is the act of reuniting the two. In the architecture from Part 1, that reunion happened through the Ads Metadata Registry , a Key-Value store: When the ad server made a decision, it wrote the metadata for that impression into the registry. It encoded only reference identifiers into the opaque token returned to the device, keeping the token small. Later, when the client fired an event carrying that token, the Ads Event Publisher decoded the token, looked up the metadata in the registry, and stitched the two together into an enriched ad event. This design served us well. The registry was globally replicated, which gave us a useful property almost for free: an event arriving in any region could find its metadata regardless of where the ad was decided. It future-proofed the token against ever-growing metadata, and it carried us through the first phase of Netflix’s advertising growth. The ad server writes per-impression metadata to the globally replicated registry on the serving path, and the Ads Event Publisher reads it back to enrich each client event. But as we looked ahead, especially to ads on live streams, the limits of this design became clear. Why we needed to evolve The forcing function was Live. title: Netflix Conductor: The Next Chapter
abstract: Netflix Conductor : The Next Chapter by Aravindan Ramkumar on behalf of the Conductor team Conductor is the workflow orchestration engine Netflix uses to stitch micro-services into reliable, observable business processes. If you’ve followed Conductor from the outside, the last thing you heard was probably the note on its GitHub repository : Netflix discontinued maintenance of Conductor OSS to refocus its resources on the internal fork. That announcement marked the end of the open-source chapter, and from the outside it may have looked like the end of the story. It wasn’t. Internally, Conductor never slowed down. If anything, it grew faster, and the demands of that growth pushed us to rebuild it from the ground up. This post is the answer to the natural question that announcement leaves open: what happened to Conductor after that? A lot, it turns out. The clearest way to put it is in terms of growth. Not long ago, Conductor crossing a billion workflow executions in a single year felt like a milestone. Today it clears that bar roughly every quarter , and the monthly volume is still climbing. Sustaining that kind of growth meant rethinking nearly every layer of the system. The data plane it runs on was modernized piece by piece. The evaluation engine was rewritten. The way it allocates work, controls concurrency, and runs compute all changes. The through-line is simple: scale forced a rethink of the evaluation engine and the layers beneath it, and everything else followed. The rest of this post walks through that evolution: how the architecture changed, the performance and scale work at the heart of it, the leap forward in developer experience, and the newer capabilities for controlling how workflows and tasks execute. How Netflix uses Conductor When we last wrote about Conductor, it ran a few hundred workflow definitions for a few dozen teams. That footprint has grown by orders of magnitude. Conductor now backs roughly 200,000 workflow definitions owned by around 150 applications , spanning Content and Studio Engineering, Ads, Games, and more. The runtime side has grown to match. In a typical month it executes on the order of 420 million workflows , and on a given day it runs anywhere from 5 to 20 million , with teams adding hundreds of new workflow types every month. Conductor and the Media Production Suite One of the clearest ways to see what Conductor does is Netflix’s Media Production Suite (MPS) . It’s a set of applications that move production data into the cloud. An average Netflix title generates around 200 terabytes of original camera files, and MPS is what gets that media ingested, validated, transcoded, and delivered to the right people around the world. The multi-step pipelines behind MPS’s workflows (Footage Ingest, Dailies, VFX Pulls, and Conform Pulls) run as Conductor workflows. A dedicated orchestration layer called Studio Orchestrator stitches together the platform services these pipelines depend on, such as asset management, media encoding, and storage, using Conductor under the hood to ensure reliable execution and the durability to recover from the inevitable failures of long-running, distributed work. Beyond the studio: Ads and Games Content engineering is where Conductor started, but it’s no longer the whole story. Two of Netflix’s newer businesses lean on it just as heavily. Netflix Ads has made Conductor a backbone of its programmatic pipelines. Creative ingestion, advertiser-certificate management, and privacy-preserving Data Clean Rooms all run as Conductor workflows. Netflix Games uses Conductor to orchestrate the path a game takes from a partner’s submission to the app stores. When a studio uploads a build, a Conductor pipeline ingests the binary, runs the required validations (for example, iOS privacy-manifest checks), and drives App Store publishing, coordinating steps that span multiple platform services and external stores with the same reliability and visibility the studio pipelines rely on. title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
abstract: By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile. A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result. That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way. The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks. While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely. To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it. The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow , Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development : our workflows run on Maestro ( Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment , then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs. With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment . I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job. Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required. The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging.
