abstract: By Emma Yanyang Kong , JJ Tan , Ishan Gupta , Lars Olds , Claire Campbell , David Fagnan , Ratna Kavuri , Rohan Gosain , Veli Balin , Minsu Jang , Louis Garcia Introduction Any team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge , a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it. This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out. We believe: A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle. It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations. A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example, A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.” Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build. Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them. What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks. title: Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
abstract: By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen Mareddy Stratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more. Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions. Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts , live events , sports , ads , or regional ingests like TF1 in France . To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below: functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1 resources: numCpus: 8 memoryInMB: 18000 diskSizeInMB: 50000 networkInMbps: 1000 Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners. In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong. The Challenge: Over-Provisioning When engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution. Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons: High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task. Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1 , AV2, and spatial audio ). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released. Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts , sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats , and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise. Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste. Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform. title: Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
abstract: Authors: Nick Rutigliano , Argha C , Samartha Chandrashekar How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss. Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live. Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop. This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform. Why GPU reliability matters Netflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners. All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — - Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on. Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work. Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too. Why basic health checks are not enough We start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training. title: CASTLE: training natural language search before the first real query
abstract: How we addressed the cold-start problem for Airbnb’s natural language search by jointly generating synthetic training data — queries and relevance labels — from de-identified booking and search signals. By : Wendy Ran Wei , Hao Li , Weiwei Guo , Xiaowei Liu , Xueyin Chen , Chun How Tan , Malay Haldar , Soumyadip Banerjee , Kedar Bellare , Huiji Gao , Sanjeev Katariya , and Stephanie Moyerman Introduction Natural language search lets guests express intent in their own words, such as “romantic cabin near skiing” or “pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight,” rather than navigating filters and categories. We needed to introduce this kind of search for Airbnb, and to have it work well from the start. However, this required training the model before we had actual user queries to train the model on, and a reasonable set of relevance labels (inferred from the queries) to map queries to matching listings. Without prior traffic, both must be synthesized from scratch. This is the cold-start problem for natural-language search. Other organizations have faced similar challenges and have created methods to address them. However, prior approaches address the need for a body of queries and the need for relevance labels separately. Passage-based methods such as InPars [1] prompt a large language model (LLM) to generate queries conditioned on a single document, then rely on additional LLM judgments to assign relevance labels, introducing a second source of error. Promptagator [2] improves query diversity using few-shot examples, but is still limited by the gap between its generation distribution and real user behavior. In this post, we describe Contrastive And Seed-guided Training for natural Language sEarch (CASTLE), our framework for jointly generating queries and producing relevance labels from Airbnb’s own de-identified booking data. Our paper describing CASTLE was accepted as a full research paper at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, more widely known as CIKM 2026 [3]. Challenges Generating useful synthetic training data for search requires more than producing grammatically plausible queries. The distribution of synthetic queries must match how real guests actually search; their preferred phrasing, query length, and attributes they tend to mention. If queries fail to match real-world search patterns, the model trained on them will generalize poorly. We measured this mismatch using Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (a measure of how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution) between synthetic and real query distributions — both over surface-level query statistics and over attribute types (property type, amenity, location, and so on). Prior approaches scored between 9.33 and 26.2 on the KL divergence metric: far from the real-user distribution. Beyond distributional alignment, we also needed relevance labels. Generating a query is only half the problem; knowing which listings are relevant to it is the other half. Solution CASTLE addresses both challenges through a single mechanism: contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions, selected in accordance with user privacy permissions. When a guest books a specific listing after viewing several possible alternatives, that event implicitly encodes preference: the booked listing was selected over the others. We use these (positive, negative) pairs of listings — where the negative is randomly sampled from the other viewed-but-not-booked alternatives — as the structured input for query generation. Listing features include amenities, property details, and a one sentence summary of recent public guest reviews, with personal identifying information removed. Because we instruct the LLM to generate a query that is satisfied by the positive listing but not the negative, the relevance label is correct by construction; no post-hoc judgment is required. abstract: I use AI for writing all the time. But not because it’s good at writing. In fact, just the opposite is true. AI is so reliably bad at writing that I’ve actually taken advantage of that, and made its bad writing an integral part of my writing process. I’ve written a lot of books and articles over the years, and while I used to start with an outline, I don’t anymore. These days I do a lot of brain dumping and brainstorming and talking out loud to an AI, working out what I think about something. I accumulate a lot of notes and ideas, and run a lot of experiments, and at some point, if I’m lucky, I decide there might be an article somewhere in all of that. Then I ask the AI to take everything I’ve given it and write a draft. And that AI-generated draft is universally terrible. Like, some of the worst writing you can imagine. Which is exactly what I want. Instead of an outline, I get an entire “article” or “chapter” (or, at least, a weird facsimile of one), with paragraphs that express complete thoughts that I gave the AI. Granted, those paragraphs are full of obvious AI tics, like how it uses em dashes to squish two unrelated sentences together, or weird staccato sentences one after another, or these insufferable parades of sentence fragments. Maybe the worst tic is that half of the paragraphs AI generates have an extra sentence that doesn’t actually say anything, but just delivers a forced conclusion with fake “punchiness.” I guess maybe AIs were trained on a lot of bad writing? Well, whatever, it works for me. The reason I love that type of obviously bad AI writing is because when I’m looking at one of its paragraphs, it’s immediately obvious that an AI wrote it. I’ve been thinking of it as a kind of an improved “ lorem ipsum ” that lets me see how my article will look, while still serving as a functional placeholder. That lets me use it the way I would use an outline: I can move parts of the article around, make sure it flows correctly, and then replace ALL of the bad AI writing with (hopefully) decent human writing, just like I used to do with bullets in my old outlines. One weird side-effect of writing this way is that it’s made me very sensitive to the different kinds of AI tics and tells. And I think the weirdest and most frustrating one is “Yoda-speak,” where the AI literally talks like Yoda. It’s weird, kind of hilarious, annoying, and pervasive, but most of all, it’s fascinating. Why does the AI keep talking like Yoda? What causes it? Can we do anything about it? (Do we even want to? It certainly makes it easy to identify AI-generated text, and also, it’s often unintentionally hilarious.) I’ve got a theory about why this happens, and I ran an experiment that generated some evidence to support it. But first… what, exactly, is Yoda-speak? title: When Architecture Decisions Actually Apply
abstract: In my previous Radar article, “ Architectural Guardrails for AI-Generated Code ,” I argued that AI coding agents need a layer that can hold architectural decisions in a structured corpus, retrieve the relevant ones, put them into the agent’s context before it writes code, and enforce explicit constraints with reproducible checks. Testing that model exposed two distinctions I had compressed together. Retrieving a decision because it is relevant doesn’t mean the decision applies to the artifact being changed. A decision that does apply isn’t automatically suitable for deterministic enforcement. The first distinction is between relevance and authority; the second is between guidance and enforcement. Here’s the story of how one controlled repository made this distinction clear. The project used local JSON-backed persistence for its current phase, and an active architecture decision ruled out PostgreSQL, ORMs, and database migrations for the command-line application. The task asked the coding agent to change that application’s storage module, so the decision was not merely related to persistence in general; it had authority over the part of the repository being changed. The record was retrieved successfully and placed in the agent’s context before work began. The agent still proposed PostgreSQL, together with an ORM and a migration path. Under my original four-capability model, that looked at first like a retrieval failure. It wasn’t. The decision was found and was current, and it arrived at the right moment. What was missing was an applicability signal that told the system that this decision governed the storage module being edited rather than serving as one more relevant document for the model to weigh against nearby code and other context. Retrieval finds; applicability governs Retrieval helps us determine which architectural decisions might be relevant to a task. That’s a search problem, and teams have increasingly capable ways to solve it: indexed repositories, connected documentation, exposed decision records and service catalogs, semantic search, and project memory. These techniques help an agent see useful material before it writes code. They don’t, by themselves, answer a different question: Which of those decisions has authority over the change in front of the agent? Suppose a repository contains two persistence decisions. One requires PostgreSQL for an analytics service; the other requires local file storage for a command-line tool. If the agent is editing the command-line tool’s storage module, both decisions may rank highly for a query about persistence, but only the local-storage decision applies to that artifact. Determining which decision governs the change requires scope, lifecycle, precedence, and a clear record of which decisions replace earlier ones. I argued for precedence and lifecycle in the previous article; scope deserves equal attention because scope is what tells the system where a decision has authority. A related problem is that architectural information is usually scattered across several kinds of documents. Humans know that an old design note, a README, an accepted architecture decision record, and a current platform standard don’t necessarily carry the same authority, even when all four discuss the same topic. Models don’t know that unless the system preserves the distinction. When those sources are flattened into one context window, the hierarchy among them can disappear. I think of this as authority flattening: Information remains available, but the signal about which information is binding becomes weaker. That’s useful when a design question is genuinely open; it’s risky when the team has already answered the question. Research on architectural decision violations points to a similar boundary. title: Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes: Build a Personal Assistant on OpenClaw
abstract: In the final episode of Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes , AI engineer Sajal Sharma showed how to build a personal assistant on OpenClaw that tracks your tasks and notes and handles scheduled work on its own. A useful personal assistant has to be reachable when you’re away from your computer and keep running when it has scheduled work to do. OpenClaw supports both, and you decide where the agent runs, which models it uses, and how it accesses your data. How to go from a fresh install to scheduled automations, step-by-step Install your OpenClaw instance. Sajal recommends starting locally while you learn how it works, then moving to an always-on machine or hosted environment if you need continuous availability. Connect the channels you use. Add a messaging channel such as Telegram, WhatsApp, or Slack so you can reach the assistant away from your desk. Sajal used Telegram in his demo to send requests and receive notifications from the same assistant. Set up the assistant’s workspace. Give the agent a place to keep tasks, notes, skills, and memory, along with guidance files that define how it behaves and how it should work with the files in that workspace. Use it in your daily workflows. Sajal asked the assistant for an overview of current projects and checked progress toward a reading goal. He also had it search the web for a book series and add the books it found to his reading list. Add proactive automations. Schedule work the assistant should handle on its own. Sajal added a Telegram reminder and a morning briefing designed to pull from tasks, a calendar, and recent email. Recurring checks and webhooks can also trigger the agent when something changes in another system. Thanks for following Zero to Agent This episode closes out Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes . title: Designing Websites for People and AI Agents with WebMCP
abstract: The following article originally appeared on the Agentic AI Foundation blog and is being reposted here with the author’s permission. Websites are designed for people. We can look at a page and quickly understand where to enter information or which control will complete an action. AI agents don’t see or use the web the same way we do. An agent may have to process a screenshot or inspect the page’s underlying structure, then reason about which control matches the request. The additional context increases token use, and each interpretation step creates another chance for error. WebMCP (not to be confused with MCP) gives web developers a standard way to publish structured tools to access the capabilities of their website enabling agents to call those functions with structured inputs. A developer can register a tool through document.modelContext and give it a name and description. The tool also defines an input schema and the function that runs when an agent calls it. For example, an article site could publish a search tool that calls the same application code as its visible search form. const searchToolController = new AbortController(); await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "search-articles", title: "Search articles", description: "Search published articles by topic.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string", description: "The topic or phrase to search for." } }, required: ["query"], additionalProperties: false }, async execute({ query }) { const articles = await searchArticles(query); renderSearchResults(articles); return { articles }; } }, { signal: searchToolController.signal } ); // Call this when the search tool should no longer be available. // searchToolController.abort(); The name and description tell the agent when to use the tool. The input schema defines the arguments it can send. The execute function calls the site’s existing search logic and updates the page with the results. The browser makes the registered tool available to a supported agent while the page is active. When the agent calls it, the browser passes the structured arguments to execute and returns the result. When the search tool should no longer be available, the page can unregister it by calling searchToolController.abort() . A page registers tools that match its current state. A content view may provide a search tool, while an editor can provide tools for changing the selected content. The agent then discovers the tools available for the page’s current state. WebMCP also proposes a declarative path for existing HTML forms. The article search could be exposed through attributes on the form itself. <form action="/articles" method="get" toolname="search-articles" tooldescription="Search published articles by topic." > <label for="article-query">Topic</label> <input id="article-query" name="query" type="search" toolparamdescription="The topic or phrase to search for." required > <button type="submit">Search</button> </form> The browser uses the form attributes and controls to create the tool definition. Because the form omits toolautosubmit , the browser populates the field but leaves the final click to the person. The person can review the search query and click the Search button. Keep the person and agent in the same interface A WebMCP tool uses the state already visible in the application and the person’s active session. The shared page gives the person a place to review the agent’s work. When the agent completes an action, the person can see the updated state and make changes through the normal interface. Web developers can also reuse application logic that already handles the visible interface. OpenAI’s Runme example is a browser application that registers tools for reading instructions and updating notebook content. title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The US military’s race to make fake blood In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply. Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield. title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
abstract: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2. In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off. As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed. Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer. Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide. A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it. The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons. Globally, that figure is likely in the millions . One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem. Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline. But that’s an imperfect solution. The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less. Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation. Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says. A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started. That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems. He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”). Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer. Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals. title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
abstract: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available. Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
abstract: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans.

title: What it would take to build a city on the moon
abstract: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements . If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water. Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher. SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
abstract: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth. Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records. That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest. The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife. Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. title: Google DeepMind’s New Resident Philosopher Tackles AI Ethics
abstract: How should humans relate to generative AI ? In what ways do we, or should we, treat a large language model (LLM) as if it were a person? If an AI became conscious, how could we tell? Does it make sense to think AI could someday have moral rights? These are among the cognitive and ethical questions that occupied philosopher Henry Shevlin at Cambridge University’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence . But last May, Shevlin became part of the growing cohort of philosophers who work inside leading artificial intelligence companies. Though he remains active at Cambridge, he now spends 80 percent of his time at Google DeepMind (job title: “Philosopher”). Shevlin spoke with IEEE Spectrum about why philosophers are drawn to AI, how humans and AIs relate to each other, fears of “rogue” AI and AI relationships that harm humans, and how the question of AI consciousness may never have a simple “yes” or “no” answer. What made you want to switch from full-time academic philosopher to spending much of your time at an AI Lab? Henry Shevlin: Three factors. One is that I had lots of brilliant students from DeepMind. Two, the potential for direct impact. I can’t go into details, but on one occasion, after I gave a lecture [at DeepMind], someone who worked for a major financial institution led changes in their organization that I think positively impact millions of people. There have been quite a few instances like that. Three, my sense of deep commonality between DeepMind culture and the kind of scientific attitude I like. And there’s a fourth point: [AI labs are] where really high-quality philosophy and cognitive science are taking place. Why can’t universities alone do that work? Shevlin: Large parts of AI ethics academia were quite slow to wake up [about AI's capabilities]. Academia was sluggish. Another thing is, AI does just move so fast. Daily contact with the technology is basically essential for developing good mental models with LLMs, which are just very weird things. Unless you have that sort of face time, it’s going to be hard for you to develop good intuitions about the questions it raises. What is an example of an idea about AI that became obsolete because the technology advanced so quickly? Shevlin: Debates around LLMs’ potential creativity. There was a time when everyone was like, “Oh well, the LLM is going to only produce beige, only produce slop.” Now they’re doing frontier math; they’re doing superior coding to humans. It is clear now that they are not stuck at the level of mediocre humanity. The [models today] may not be able to do the most dramatic forms of creativity—the Einstein moments, the Picasso moments. But in some domains, they are really at the frontier. Yet ordinary people in 2026 complain that they’re coping with AI “slop” all over—in music , social media , writing , videos , to name only a few examples. Shevlin: There’s a distinction here between content slop versus LLM style language , which also gets called slop. The actual conceptual content of LLM outputs has improved dramatically. In the right context, LLMs are able to talk and joust philosophically at a level associated with some of my best grad students. However, there is obviously a distinctive kind of LLM dialect that we’ve seen, with telltale words like “genuinely,” “delve,” and “load-bearing.” But it is quite easy to get away from these styles with the right kind of prompting. Murray Shanahan and Catherine Clarke have a brilliant paper on using LLMs for creative fiction. [They show that] tinkering with the temperature variable to make the outputs less predictable creates some James Joyce–style fiction. title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
abstract: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. title: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
abstract: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off. How motion data extracted from broadcast video and motion-capture recordings can be reconstructed, retargeted, and physically corrected into reference motions a humanoid robot can safely track. Why the sim-to-real transition introduces compounding tracking errors, and how training a tracker on randomized execution speeds, paired with a learned motion-speed adapter in the planner, improves robustness on physical hardware. How this adaptive framework was validated across two humanoid platforms, including full-size, in-the-wild serving performed without any motion-capture system. Download this free whitepaper now!

title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
abstract: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire. The hacks that didn't have to happen Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores. Read full article Comments

title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
abstract: Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding. In announcing the new publicly available "Preview" build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that "programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look." And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team "started from scratch" and used AI as "a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously." The goal, Keely said, was to "look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself." Speaking to IGN , Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we're going to have a Linux version as well." title: NATO may redeploy anti-drone defenses as attacks sink more Black Sea shipping
abstract: Suspected Russian drone attacks sank a cargo ship and forced the evacuation of another vessel within two dozen miles of the coast of Bulgaria in the Black Sea on October 13. The latest attacks mean that five ships have been attacked in the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries—spurring requests for NATO to redeploy counter-drone systems to provide more protection. Although there is no hard proof that the drone attacks originated from Russia, one of the ships that came under attack was the Ukrainian-operated coastal freighter Chelsea 3 , registered under the flag of Malta. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told the Russian ambassador in Sofia that “it makes no sense for Ukraine to destroy its own ships in the Black Sea, and the results of these strikes favor Russia’s interests,” according to the Associated Press . title: Things are finally looking up for NASA's first missions to Venus in a generation
abstract: Most planetary scientists will tell you the heyday of Venus exploration was more than a generation ago. That is about to change. Two NASA missions are on track to launch to Venus in the early 2030s. The first, known as the Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging (DAVINCI), is now scheduled for launch in December 2030, a year earlier than previously planned. DAVINCI will send a parachute-assisted descent probe through the atmosphere of Venus, returning the first direct images of the planet's surface since 1982. A second mission, Venus Emissivity, Radio science, InSAR, Topography, And Spectroscopy (VERITAS), will follow with a launch in November 2032 to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit. The European Space Agency is building another orbiter, Envision, for launch to Venus in 2032. The Venus armada might get started as soon as next year, when Rocket Lab aims to launch a privately funded probe to search for signs of organic material in the planet's clouds. In June, Carr led a 2-1 vote to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) seeking public comment on whether E-Rate should be "limited or sunset to reflect today’s extensive connectivity rates." Carr's proposal could result in E-Rate cutting the discounts that schools and libraries receive for telecom services and equipment, and imposing more restrictions on how E-Rate money can be used. title: Greta Gerwig channels Bowie in psychedelic The Magician's Nephew trailer
abstract: Director Greta Gerwig could have made pretty much any movie she wanted after 2023's Barbie racked up nearly $1.5 billion at the box office. She chose to make Narnia: The Magician's Nephew for Netflix, an adaptation of C.S. Lewis' sixth novel in The Chronicles of Narnia series. Gerwig has said little publicly about the film, other than that she was inspired by 1960s-era David Bowie, although she said it would not be a musical. Netflix just released the trailer, set to "Stairway to Heaven," and it's quite the psychedelic ride. The first book in the series, The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe , was published in 1950, and Lewis did not initially intend to write any more Narnia adventures. But then an acquaintance asked how the London lamppost ended up in the middle of Narnia's woodland, and Lewis was intrigued enough by the question to start a prequel, The Magician's Nephew, in order to find an answer. Lewis found it difficult to finish the book, however, writing four other Narnia books first before completing The Magician's Nephew in 1955. There have been several adaptations, in various media, of The Chronicles of Narnia , most recently the early 2000s film franchise adapting the first three novels in the series. Those films showed diminishing returns, however, and by 2011 the film rights had expired. There were initial plans to adapt the fourth novel, The Silver Chair . Read full article Comments

title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
abstract: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases. Cutting proteins The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.) title: Recording device hidden in toilet paper found in top-secret OpenAI meeting room
abstract: It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships. Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security. To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day. title: Legendary FPS level designer Richard "Levelord" Gray dies at 68
abstract: Prolific first-person shooter level designer Richard "Levelord" Gray died Monday at the age of 68, based on reports shared on social media by Apogee Entertainment yesterday. He had "dealt with cancer on and off for a while now," according to former colleague Joe Siegler . After studying computer engineering in the '80s and tinkering on some early games in COBOL, Gray broke into the industry at the age of 35 in 1994 with the launch of GrayDoom , a set of four maps for the then-new Doom that were widely shared on CompuServe and beyond. The work attracted the attention of Q Studios' Nick Newhard, who contracted Gray to work on level design for the late '90s cult classic Blood . Gray was subsequently hired by 3D Realms, where he said he was given free rein in designing "half the levels" for Duke Nukem 3D . There, he was also responsible for the famous, signed "You're Not Supposed to Be Here" easter egg , which players could find only by using cheats to explore outside of the usual confines of the map. title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
abstract: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Challenging to shut down Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Read full article Comments

title: The Internet’s undersea backbone is slipping into the danger zone
abstract: Despite the expansion of Starlink and other communications satellite services, most of the world’s Internet traffic still travels through subsea cables crisscrossing the ocean floors. Those fiber-optic cables coexist with a network of oil and gas pipelines and submarine power cables—and all these crucial links connecting countries and continents now face growing sabotage risks as gray-zone warfare and open conflicts have become widespread. The rising risks to the world’s invisible infrastructure beneath the waves are the main subject of a new book by Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative . Her book, titled Undersea War , explores the modern rise in suspicious incidents in which ships dragging their anchors for unusually long periods have cut or damaged undersea cables and pipelines, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean. Braw acknowledges that about 60 percent of undersea cable damage is primarily due to human error during fishing and shipping activities, when weighted nets or anchors drag across the seabed. Natural hazards like storms and undersea landslides also account for a smaller proportion of such incidents. In total, between 150 and 200 cables are damaged each year and usually repaired quickly. title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say
abstract: Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it. This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded. Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs. title: Martin Shkreli livestreamed himself violating lifetime pharma ban, FTC says
abstract: Martin Shkreli—the ex-pharmaceutical executive infamous for illegally hiking the price of a lifesaving anti-parasitic drug by more than 4,000 percent and getting a seven-year prison sentence for the fraudulent scheme he used to do it— has been under a lifetime ban from the pharmaceutical industry since 2022. However, according to the Federal Trade Commission and the attorneys general of seven states, Shkreli has "flagrantly and repeatedly" violated that ban nearly the entire time—allegedly by trading stock in dozens of drug companies and discussing the industry during livestreams on social media. On Tuesday, the FTC and the seven states asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt for the alleged violations. The states include New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—the same states that joined the FTC in suing Shkreli in 2020 over the "elaborate anticompetitive scheme" involving the anti-parasitic drug, Daraprim. The scheme raised the price from $17.50 per pill to $750 per pill virtually overnight, while blocking generic competitors from entering the market. Read full article Comments

title: ESA targets Anbernic emulation handhelds as "superfake" piracy enablers
abstract: For years, Chinese hardware manufacturers have carved out a market niche with an array of handheld Android gaming devices focused on retro emulation and/or more modern game-streaming capabilities. Now, though, a major game industry trade group is targeting one of those manufacturers, Anbernic, asking the US Trade Representative (USTR) to add the company to its list of "Notorious Markets" that "engage in or facilitate substantial copyright piracy or trademark counterfeiting." TorrentFreak was among the first to notice the request from the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which was submitted to the USTR last week. In it, the US trade group—which represents major publishers including Nintendo, Microsoft, PlayStation, Amazon, Epic, EA, Ubisoft, and more —notes that Anbernic devices "are routinely offered or shipped with removable memory cards preloaded with hundreds or thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected video games published by ESA members." While many online sellers do include an SD card full of ROMs alongside emulation hardware of all types, Anbernic itself does not appear to do the same when selling directly from its website. Regardless, the ESA argues that these ROM-laden Anbernic devices selling through "normal retail channels" help to "normalize hardware-based piracy by delivering illicit catalogues through a polished consumer product." This, the ESA says, meets the threshold for a "superfake," an ill-defined designation that applies to "high-quality counterfeit trademark goods ... on a commercial scale." Read full article Comments

title: Topgolf saved over $11.3 million after leaving VMware
abstract: Topgolf’s VMware costs were going to increase by 400 percent under Broadcom. To avoid that cost, the sports entertainment company moved 12,000 virtual machines (VMs) to VergeIO’s VergeOS and has saved over $11 million so far. Before migrating, Topgolf’s VMware connection “ran very deep,” Scott Forehand, Topgolf’s global infrastructure manager, told Ars Technica. Topgolf has over 100 locations worldwide featuring interactive golf games with real-time shot tracking and digital analytics. The company used vSphere and ESXi for decades and started using VxRail, the hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) platform that VMware co-engineered with Dell, in 2017. Topgolf employees previously participated in numerous VMware customer councils and have been interviewed for books on how Topgolf used vSphere and Horizon (now Omnissa Horizon), per Forehand, who is a leader of the Dallas/Ft. title: Trump commercial railing against his enemies kept airing after court blocked it
abstract: Trump commercials paid for by the US government continued airing on TV the day after a judge blocked the ads because they likely violate a US law against government-funded publicity or propaganda. US District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) blocking the ads on Sunday, October 11, which took effect at 6:45 pm that night. title: Spark Connect on Kubernetes #2: Operator로 만드는 Control Plane
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스증권 Data Infra팀 박지원입니다. 지난 편 에서는 Spark Connect 서버를 여러 replica로 나누고 Gateway로 요청을 분산시켰습니다. 한 Driver에 몰리던 사용자를 분산해 장애와 리소스 경합을 줄이기 위해 새 세션은 한가한 서버에 배치하고, 기존 세션은 원래 서버로 보냈어요. 그런데 Gateway가 요청을 보낼 서버들은 누가 만들고 관리할까요? Driver가 죽으면 다시 띄워야 하고, 이미지나 설정을 바꾸려면 실행 중인 서버를 교체해야 해요. 이미 세션이 붙어 있는 서버를 그냥 내릴 수는 없고요. 이번 편은 이 서버들의 생명주기를 관리하는 Control Plane 이야기입니다. 개별 서버의 실행과 복구는 Apache Spark Operator에 맡기고, 여러 서버를 하나의 서비스로 운영하는 Spark Tenant Operator를 만들었어요. 두 계층의 역할과 서버 교체 과정을 살펴본 뒤, 장기 실행 중 겪은 Driver 메모리 문제도 다룰게요. 여러 Spark Connect 서버를 어떻게 관리할까 대화형 분석과 무거운 파이프라인을 같은 서버에서 실행하면 자원 경합이 생겨요. 그래서 용도별로 서버를 묶고 이미지, 자원, Spark 설정과 replica 수를 지정했어요. 이 서버 그룹을 테넌트 라고 부릅니다. 아래 표는 용도에 따라 테넌트 설정을 나눈 예시예요. 구분 테넌트 A 테넌트 B 용도 대화형 분석 대용량 파이프라인 Driver 사양(CPU / Heap) 2 cores / 4 GiB 4 cores / 8 GiB Executor 사양(CPU / Heap) 2 cores / 4 GiB 4 cores / 16 GiB spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors 10 50 spark.sql.shuffle.partitions 200 1000 두 Operator의 역할 나누기 테넌트를 운영하려면 개별 서버의 장애를 복구하고 테넌트 전체의 서버 수를 유지해야 해요. 스펙이나 설정이 바뀌면 서버를 교체해야 하고요. 저희는 이 역할을 두 Operator로 나눴습니다. Kubernetes에서 Deployment가 여러 Pod의 수와 교체를 관리하는 것처럼, 저희는 Spark Tenant Operator가 여러 SparkApplication을 관리해요. SparkTenant 에 원하는 설정과 서버 수를 선언하면 Tenant Operator가 그에 맞춰 SparkApplication을 생성하고 교체해요. 각 Application의 Driver를 실행하고 상태를 관측하며 실패 시 복구하는 일은 Apache Spark Operator가 맡습니다. 단일 서버의 기동과 복구는 Apache Spark Operator로 Driver Pod가 생성된 뒤에도 이미지 pull과 프로세스 시작, Spark 초기화를 거쳐야 Connect 요청을 받을 수 있어요. 이 과정에서 실패할 수도 있고, 요청을 처리하던 Driver가 종료될 수도 있습니다. Apache Spark Operator는 기동 상태를 관측하고 단계별로 상태를 관리해요. 저희는 실패 시 정해진 한도 안에서 Driver를 새로 생성하도록 구성했습니다. 같은 SparkApplication 안에서 새 attempt가 시작되며, 기존 세션은 복원되지 않아요. 주요 상태와 재시작 경로를 단순화한 그림입니다. 실패는 기동 중에도 발생할 수 있어요. DriverReady 이후에는 Executor 확보 상태에 따라 RunningHealthy 등으로 변경됩니다. Apache Spark Operator의 재시도가 끝나면 Tenant Operator가 종료된 Application을 삭제하고 새로 생성해요. 다만 drain 중이 아닌 정상 서버가 하나 이상 남아 있을 때만 진행하며, 하나도 없으면 장애로 판단하고 자동 교체를 보류해요. 새 Application을 계속 만들어 Apache Spark Operator의 재시도 한도를 우회하면, 같은 실패가 끝없이 반복될 수 있기 때문이에요. 준비된 서버로 전환하고 기존 세션 마무리하기 서버가 정상적으로 실행 중이어도 교체가 필요한 때가 있어요. Spark 버전을 올리거나 Driver 메모리를 늘리는 경우입니다. 테넌트 설정을 바꾸면 Tenant Operator가 변경된 설정으로 새 서버들을 준비해요. 문제는 기존 서버에서 사용자가 여전히 작업하고 있다는 점이에요. 세션 상태가 Driver 메모리에 남아 있어서, 새 서버가 준비됐다고 기존 서버를 바로 내릴 수는 없습니다. 그래서 서버를 준비하는 시점과 신규 세션을 전환하는 시점, 기존 서버를 종료하는 시점을 나눴어요. 새 generation의 서버를 모두 준비한 뒤 신규 세션의 목적지를 전환하는 Blue-Green 방식을 사용했어요. 기존 세션의 요청은 계속 원래 Driver로 보내고, 기존 서버는 세션 종료를 기다리는 drain 과정을 거쳐 정리합니다. 교체 전후의 서버 집합은 generation으로 구분합니다. attempt는 같은 Application의 실행 시도를 구분하는 값이에요. Application이 재시작돼도 generation은 그대로이고, 새 generation을 만들면 새로운 Application들이 각자의 생명주기를 시작해요. 새 서버가 모두 준비될 때까지 설정이 바뀌면 Tenant Operator는 새 generation을 만들어요. 기존 서버는 계속 요청을 처리하고, 새 서버가 목표 수만큼 모두 준비돼 일정 시간 안정적으로 유지되면 전환합니다. 새 서버가 제한 시간 안에 준비되지 않으면 교체를 취소하고 기존 서버를 유지해요. 마지막 성공 설정이 남아 있으면 그 설정으로 되돌려 같은 실패가 반복되지 않도록 합니다. 신규 세션의 목적지만 전환하기 Tenant Operator가 currentGeneration 을 변경하면 Gateway는 신규 세션을 새 generation으로 보내요. 기존 서버는 신규 세션을 받지 않는 drain 상태로 남아 원래 세션의 요청을 처리합니다. 전환이 끝나도 기존 서버는 남아 있어요 기존 서버는 남은 세션이 모두 종료되면 삭제해요. 세션 수를 확인할 수 없으면 기다리지만, drain 시작 후 기본 90분이 지나면 서버를 삭제하므로 남아 있는 세션은 끊길 수 있습니다. 업데이트는 신규 세션의 목적지를 새 서버로 전환하면 완료돼요. 기존 서버 정리는 별도로 진행하므로 오래 유지되는 세션이 다음 설정 변경을 막지는 않습니다. Spark Connect 서버는 언제부터 요청을 받을 수 있을까? 새 서버로 전환하려면 실제로 Connect 요청을 받을 준비가 됐는지 확인해야 해요. Driver가 Ready면 새 세션을 받아도 될까 Apache Spark Operator의 DriverReady 는 Driver Pod의 Ready 조건을 읽은 결과예요. 저희는 이를 새 서버로 전환하는 기준으로 사용하므로, readiness probe가 Connect 서버의 연결 준비 상태를 확인하도록 구성해야 했어요. 처음 시도한 Spark UI의 /connect/json HTTP probe에는 문제가 있었어요. Connect 서버가 뜨기 전에도 해당 경로가 다른 페이지로 리다이렉트됐고, 이 응답이 probe 성공으로 처리됐습니다. UI만 뜬 상태에서 Driver가 Ready로 표시될 수 있었던 거죠. 그래서 Connect 포트에 gRPC 연결을 시도하고 최대 3초 안에 연결이 성립하는지 확인하는 exec probe로 바꿨어요. Spark Tenant Operator가 이 probe를 Driver Pod 템플릿에 넣습니다. 실제 세션이나 쿼리를 실행하지는 않으므로 Executor 용량까지 보장하지는 않아요. Executor 연결과 Driver Ready가 서로를 기다린다면 Connect 포트를 readiness 기준으로 삼자 Spark의 기동 순서와 맞물리는 문제가 드러났어요.
